title: Why Blockbuster Didn't Buy Netflix for $50 Million
description:
In 2000, Netflix's co-founders say they offered to sell the company to Blockbuster for $50 million, and Blockbuster said no (Blockbuster's former CEO later said there were never serious talks). Blockbuster peaked at about 9,100 stores in 2004 and filed for bankruptcy in September 2010. Netflix moved from DVDs by mail to streaming, and in 2025 brought in $45.2 billion, about 904 times that asking price, with over 325 million paid memberships. The lesson: protect the future, not just this year's profits.

Sources: Marc Randolph, 'That Will Never Work' (2019); Reed Hastings & Erin Meyer, 'No Rules Rules' (2020); Newsweek fact check (updated Feb 2, 2022); Netflix Form S-1 (SEC, Mar 6, 2002), 2000 revenue $35.9M and net loss $57.4M; Associated Press (Sept 23, 2010) on Blockbuster's bankruptcy and 2004 store peak; Netflix Q4 2025 shareholder letter (Jan 20, 2026). Educational content, not investment advice.

scenes.say: Back then, Netflix brought in about thirty-six million dollars a year, and lost fifty-seven million.
Blockbuster's former boss later said there were never serious talks. But both Netflix co-founders describe the offer in their books.
Blockbuster peaked at about nine thousand one hundred stores in two thousand four. In September twenty ten, it filed for bankruptcy.
Netflix moved from DVDs by mail to streaming. In twenty twenty-five, it brought in forty-five billion dollars, about nine hundred times that asking price, in a single year.
The lesson: protecting this year's profits can cost you the future. Keep asking what your customers will want next.
